content: Vancomycin and teicoplanin are widely used antibiotics for the treatment of gram-positive bacterial infections, particularly those caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). However, there is ongoing debate regarding their comparative effects on kidney function, with some studies suggesting that teicoplanin may be less nephrotoxic than vancomycin. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of vancomycin versus teicoplanin in patients with confirmed or suspected infections. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additional sources, such as nephrology textbooks, review articles, and unpublished or incomplete studies, were also reviewed. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing teicoplanin to vancomycin in any language were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the studies and extracted data using standardised forms. When necessary, study investigators were contacted for missing information. A random-effects model was employed to calculate pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 24 studies involving 2,610 patients were included in the analysis. Teicoplanin was associated with a significantly lower risk of nephrotoxicity compared to vancomycin (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90). Both antibiotics demonstrated similar efficacy in terms of clinical cure (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.08), microbiological cure (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.03), and mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.30). Importantly, six studies reported no cases of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring dialysis. Adverse events were less frequent with teicoplanin. Specifically, the risk of cutaneous rash was lower (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.92), as was the risk of red man syndrome (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.59) and the overall incidence of adverse events (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.00). The reduced risk of nephrotoxicity with teicoplanin was observed in patients both with (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.88) and without concomitant aminoglycoside use (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.50). Additionally, teicoplanin demonstrated a lower risk of nephrotoxicity even when vancomycin dosing was guided by serum drug levels (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.52). In conclusion, both teicoplanin and vancomycin are effective in treating patients with proven or suspected infections. However, teicoplanin is associated with a lower incidence of adverse effects, including nephrotoxicity. No cases of AKI requiring dialysis were reported in the included studies. While it remains uncertain whether the observed differences in kidney function should dictate antibiotic selection, teicoplanin may be a reasonable choice for patients at higher risk of AKI requiring dialysis.
